q0153: Vulnerable code sneaking into your releases = third-party libraries and supply chain components. Track them with an SBOM and dependency scanning.
q0154: VoIP-specific threats: vishing (voice phishing) and SPIM (spam over instant messaging and internet telephony).
q0155: Unapproved software or services brought in by employees = shadow IT.
q0156: Checking configurations against a minimum baseline = benchmarks (such as CIS Benchmarks or DISA STIGs), often scanned automatically with SCAP tools.
q0157: A domain suddenly resolving to an IP you do not own = DNS spoofing or poisoning. ARP poisoning is local: it fakes MAC-to-IP mappings.
q0158: Using captured hashes to log in elsewhere without cracking them = pass-the-hash (lateral movement). Tools like Mimikatz scrape them from memory.
q0159: Secrets in code (API keys and passwords committed to Git) are the top accidental cloud credential leak. Use a secrets manager and repository scanning.
q0160: Checking many installed certificates against revocations = CRL (the list). Checking one certificate live as it is used = OCSP.
q0161: Smart cards or certificates for network login = EAP-TLS (mutual certificate authentication). PEAP and MS-CHAPv2 are password-based.
q0162: Rootkits hide from the OS itself; finding them takes deep, behavior-based host visibility: EDR.
q0163: Generators and ISP already covered, and it must never go down → a UPS bridges the seconds until the generators start.
q0164: Visibility and control over which cloud apps are used and what is uploaded or downloaded = CASB.
q0165: 'Log in with Google or Facebook' = OpenID Connect (authentication built on OAuth 2.0).
q0166: Central key management across clouds, using your own existing keys = HSM as a service (cloud HSM).
q0167: Random characters added before hashing = a salt. Salts defeat rainbow tables and make identical passwords hash differently.
q0168: A task fails because the account lacks permissions → least privilege is working; request the proper access rather than bypassing it.
q0169: Malware installing on hosts and moving between them → EDR (detect, block and isolate endpoints).
q0170: Suspicious traffic between internal endpoints that the perimeter firewall never sees → host-based firewalls (or microsegmentation).
q0171: Moving to the cloud: design the security architecture first, then choose providers and fit costs within it.
q0172: Protecting backups from one natural disaster = geographic dispersion (sites far apart).
q0173: Lots of odd DNS queries to the internet, especially off-hours = DNS tunneling, a data exfiltration technique.
q0174: A text message pretending to be the CEO and asking for gift cards = smishing (with impersonation).
q0175: You cannot measure exposure to a new vulnerability without knowing what you run: a full asset inventory comes first.
q0176: Push a setting to every Windows domain machine quickly = Group Policy (a GPO).
q0177: Hardening shrinks the attack surface: disable default accounts, change defaults, remove unneeded services and ports, patch.
q0178: Vestibules (mantraps), fences, locks, guards and bollards = physical controls.
q0179: Make stored data unreadable but recoverable = encryption. Hashing is one-way: for verifying, not for getting data back.
q0180: The most risk you will accept = risk threshold. Risk appetite = the general amount of risk you are willing to pursue.
q0181: Documenting who handled evidence, when and why = chain of custody.
q0182: Critical system + preventive controls available but not yet in place → mitigate by implementing them. You cannot avoid a system the business needs.
